# How Yoni got its accent back

The ASCII form *yoni* is missing something. **Yoni** restores ​the marks the source language used to distinguish this name from a thousand others — and those marks change how the name is read, pronounced, and understood. This post explains, with ‌the full scholarly record behind it, what each restored mark preserves: the Devanagari evidence, the reconstructed sound, the myths the name carries, and the mechanical logic of what each restored mark preserves. ‌By the end, the marks in Yoni will look less like ornaments and more like what they are — recovered evidence, pinned back in its proper place.

## At a Glance

- **Restored ​name:** Yoni
- **ASCII form:** yoni
- **Meaning:** "'Womb, source' — the feminine principle, the origin from which all creation flows"
- **Domain of influence:** Source, Womb, Shakti
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original ​script:** योनि (Devanagari)

## Overview

**Yoni** (*yoni*) — The Womb, the Feminine Principle · 'Womb, source' — the feminine principle, the origin from which all creation flows — belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, ​where it is catalogued under the domain "Source, Womb, Shakti". The name means "'Womb, source' — the feminine principle, the origin from which all creation flows".

**Yoni** is the source: the ​womb, the origin-place, the feminine principle that the Śaiva tradition pairs with the liṅga as the two-in-one of all generation. In philosophy it names the material cause — prakṛti, the matrix ​from which the differentiated world flows; in ritual it is the altar’s base, the goddess’s body, and the cosmic ground on which the god stands.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Yoni** and ‌serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/yoni/). The restoration aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed from the displayed form itself. The plain ASCII form *yoni* survives as a modern convenience imposed by ​the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Devanagari as **योनि**. Etymologically it means ​"'Womb, source' — the feminine principle, the origin from which all creation flows".

The ASCII form *yoni* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological ‌compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Yoni** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed ​from the displayed form itself.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **y** → **Y** — Same, capitalized
- **o** → **o** — Same
- **n** → **n** — Same
- **i** → **i** — Same

## The ‌Original Script

The name is preserved in Devanagari as **योनि**.

The scholarly transliteration is *Yoni*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Sanskrit Yoni is written in Devanagari as योनि
- IAST transliteration ​maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of ‌the name is **/ˈjoʊni/** — Sanskrit (IAST: Yoni).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Yo-** — The root is √yu, “to unite, join” — the same yu-family as yoga’s yoking.
- **-ni** — The feminine ​noun: “womb”, “source”, “place of origin”.
- **** — The feminine principle, the origin — paired with the liṅga in Śaiva worship.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: “YOH-nee”

Kindred ​and historical forms of the name:

- **Counterpart** — liṅga — the mark; together the Śaiva aniconic pair
- **Root** — √yu — to unite; the same family as yoga

The word means womb, ​source, and place of origin — the feminine as the container of creation.

## Mythology

The yoni’s mythology is the Śaiva theology of the pair: the god and his power, the liṅga ​and its base, the still and the flowing. Its narratives are the Goddess-traditions’ own — Satī’s sacrifice, the dismembered pīṭhas, and the tantric ritual in which the base is the goddess’s ​body receiving the god’s libation. The word itself is the doctrine: the womb as the world’s first fact.

### The Endless Pillar and Its Base (Liṅga Purāṇa)

The tradition’s founding image: the endless ‌pillar of fire — the liṅga without top or bottom — that humbled Brahmā and Vishnu, standing in the yoni-base as the ground of the ground. The Purāṇa’s theology is exact: ​the mark is the god, the base is his power, and worship of the one without the other is incomplete.

### The Dismembered Seat (Satī Cycle)

When Satī self-immolated at her father’s ‌insult, Śiva wandered the world with her corpse, and the pieces fell as the śakti-pīṭhas — each a seat of the goddess’s power, each in some tellings marked by the yoni. The ​tantric pilgrimages map the goddess’s body onto the subcontinent: the womb as sacred geography.

### The Rite of the Base (Tantric Ritual)

In the tantric pūjā the yoni-basin receives the libations poured ‌over the liṅga, channelling the offering to the goddess below. The ritual grammar is the theology in action: creation as the union of the standing god and the flowing ground, generation ​as worship.

### The Matrix of Causes (Sāṃkhya Philosophy)

The Sāṃkhya makes yoni technical: prakṛti, the material cause, is the womb in which all effects pre-exist — the tree in the seed, ‌the world in the matrix. The doctrine of satkāryavāda, ‘the effect pre-exists in the cause’, is the philosophy of the yoni stated as metaphysics.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Yoni ​concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The Liṅga-Yoni** — The Śaiva aniconic pair: the standing mark in the flowing base — creation ‌and its ground, united.
- **The Material Cause** — In Sāṃkhya-Yoga, prakṛti the yoni is the womb of the world — all effects pre-exist in their cause.
- **The Goddess’s Body** — In ​the Śākta traditions the yoni is the goddess herself — the pīṭha, the sacred seat of power.
- **The Ritual Base** — Every Śaiva altar’s foundation is the yoni-shaped basin, catching the libation ​that feeds the god.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material record for Yoni survives in a small number of securely identified remains, catalogued below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, and each ‌site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

The yoni’s monuments are the oldest Śaiva remains: the Gupta liṅgas with their carved bases, the Gudimallam ithyphallic Śiva, and the aniconic ‌aniconism of every village shrine’s stone pair. The pīṭha-stones of Kāmākhyā are its most charged site.

## Realm & Domain

**Yoni** is the source: the womb, the origin-place, the feminine principle that the ‌Śaiva tradition pairs with the liṅga as the two-in-one of all generation. In philosophy it names the material cause — prakṛti, the matrix from which the differentiated world flows; in ritual ​it is the altar’s base, the goddess’s body, and the cosmic ground on which the god stands.

### The Liṅga-Yoni

The Śaiva aniconic pair: the standing mark in the flowing base — ​creation and its ground, united.

### The Material Cause

In Sāṃkhya-Yoga, prakṛti the yoni is the womb of the world — all effects pre-exist in their cause.

### The Goddess’s Body

In the Śākta ‌traditions the yoni is the goddess herself — the pīṭha, the sacred seat of power.

## Across Cultures

The yoni-liṅga pair absorbed every Indian polarity — puruṣa and prakṛti, god and goddess, stillness and flow — into a single aniconic form. The tantric traditions made ​it explicit worship; the Puranic made it respectable; and the modern world received it as scandal and symbol at once, usually without the theology.

Within the Sanskrit tradition, closely related names ‌in the corpus include [[aditi|Aditi]], [[agni|Agni]], [[ambika|Ambikā]], [[amsa|Aṃśa]], [[arjuna|Arjuna]], and [[bhakti|Bhakti]].

## Cultural Legacy

The liṅga-yoni is Hinduism’s most reproduced and least understood image — the tourist’s puzzle and the theologian’s précis. ‘Yoni’ ​entered English in the nineteenth century as a learned word; and the goddess’s-seats (śakti-pīṭhas) remain the subcontinent’s most charged pilgrimage geography.

## A Meditation

Yoni: the source-word, restored in plain letters that offer no euphemism ​and need none. The lexicon holds it as the tradition does — beside the liṅga, as the ground holds the standing thing. Two syllables, the world’s first fact.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In the case of **Yoni**, the map does not lead through ​diacritics or special letters, because the source tradition wrote the name in Devanagari rather than in the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form *yoni* and the restored form share the same letters; ​the restoration is a decision about which conventional spelling should serve as the public reference.

That decision is not cosmetic. The original script attestation carries semantic and phonetic information that no romanization ​can fully reproduce. By fixing one conventional spelling as the canonical domain form, the project prevents the drift that happens when a name is romanized differently in every article, map, and ‌database. The breakdown still lists each character — **y**, **o**, **n**, **i** — so visitors can see exactly what is being carried forward and what is not. What looks like "no ​change" is, in fact, a deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, and addressable.

A domain name is a kind of publication. When **Yoni** resolves, it proves that the restored spelling is not a theoretical exercise; it ​is a working address on the public internet. Search engines can index it, language models can encounter it, and anyone who copies it from a manuscript can paste it into a browser. ‌That practical reality changes the status of the restoration. Before Unicode domains, a scholar could write the name correctly in an article while the public web flattened it to *yoni*. Now ​the public web can carry the correct form end to end. The punycode translation happens silently, so the infrastructure remains compatible while the visible name keeps its marks. That compromise — ‌human-readable restoration, machine-readable encoding — is the foundation of every PuniCodex temple.

## Restoration Notes

Restoring a name is not a single decision; it is a sequence of smaller decisions, each backed by ‌a different kind of evidence. For **Yoni**, the chain begins with the attested form in Devanagari, continues through the standard scholarly romanizations, and ends with the DNS-compatible Unicode spelling used by ​this temple. The meaning "'Womb, source' — the feminine principle, the origin from which all creation flows" anchors the name in its semantic field; without that anchor, the marks would float ​free of the figure they name. The restored form **Yoni** and the ASCII form *yoni* share the same Latin letters; the restoration here is a conventional capitalization rather than a recovery of ​lost diacritics or special characters. Those adjustments are not arbitrary styling. They follow the restoration logic the displayed form wears openly: Yoni aSCII-equivalent form. The rule is mechanical, not editorial, which ​means the same standard applies to every entry in the lexicon. A visitor who disagrees with the classification can at least see exactly which evidence produced it, because every step is ‌recorded in the Scholarly Edition. That transparency is the difference between a restoration project and a branding exercise. The name is being put back, not invented.
